title: Is this AI slop? Two months into vibe coding a Space-based RTS
author: Livid-Evidence579
selftext: I've played RTS's as long as I can remember... I'm two months in to vibe coding my own RTS and I want to get the honest opinion of the community. Is this AI slop?? This is from the actual game itself. Tell me what to improve.

comments.author: titanunveiled
comments.body: What is your work flow for models and textures?

replies.author: Livid-Evidence579
replies.body: Well I'm utilizing Claude Chad GPT in Gemini but for completely different things. I'm not using a terminal I'm just using the work stations in the chat which I know are probably get roasted to hell in these comments for... But essentially I use Gemini as the imagination and use it to give me rough drafts of different hole configurations and different station configurations I've also used it heavily to help me put together the style Bible that I'm utilizing and to piece together and to smooth out my lower and Canon Bible. Once I have my rough imaginings then I take that style Bible and I can't buy while take it over to Claude and I kind of refine it and then after I tweak it there I take that and put it into Chad GPT to kind of tie it all together. And then I'll run separate chats for different aspects of the code base that I'm working on simultaneously. But I only let Astra or opus 5.5 touch the actual code base.

I've definitely seen games with ships that were like this, so it should be fine. 

My next game is going to be an X4-Lite. I believe modularity of parts and workable surfaces can take you pretty far for space ships. The trick will be getting each faction to be coherent

replies.author: Livid-Evidence579
replies.body: That's the big hurdle I've faced throughout developing this game. You can get it to be consistent for a little bit but then it inevitably always veers off course. Have you found any consistent workflows to get around that?

replies.author: EchoingAngel
replies.body: No, the best bet is generating everything in a single "master" run, then taking them apart and drilling down the details of each. That's how I made consistent pipes for my game when there's 4 variations of the same thing. It's not a great option for more complex things, but this was the only thing Tripo could do that Meshy couldn't. Rodin might also work, but I tend to reserve it for higher detail things

replies.author: AsparagusOk8818
replies.body:
A GOOD fighting game needs incredible intentionality throughout its entire design. The characters need to look interesting; the moves need to have a sense of weight and impact; the hitboxes and hurtboxes need to be both precise and well tuned; the animations have to look not just okay, but genuinely gorgeous. 

I have no doubt someone will eventually figure out how to get all of that working with an AI, but it's not going to happen with the current generation of tools. Animations are too costly to make and don't look good enough; character designs are serviceable but uninspiring; intentionality requires time, and in this current moment most AI tool using devs are in it to save time. So there's a fundamental disconnect between the genre and the tool's use case.

replies.author: Livid-Evidence579
replies.body: Why does that equal slop to you? If an artist uses a synthesizer in their production do you consider their song slop? Almost every single person who was an artist did when that technology came out except for the people who were using it. Now look at us... I'm putting in quite a bit of effort into making sure that this is something that people would actually want to play and yes I'm using AI as a tool to craft it but I'm genuinely aiming at giving people a good gaming experience. And if I can succeed at that I don't see why it should matter what tool I use to craft it.
